title: Inflammatory Urinary Tract Diseases: Interstitial Nephritis, Pyelonephritis, and Interstitial Cystitis
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers inflammation that targets the renal interstitium, tubules, papillae, and bladder rather than the glomeruli: drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy with papillary necrosis, chronic and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, and interstitial cystitis. Board questions usually give a drug history, a scarred or enlarged kidney, a urine sediment, or sterile bladder pain and ask for the lesion, its mechanism, and its effect on renal function. The unifying idea is that inflammation between the tubules impairs tubular work first, so concentrating ability fails, the urine fills with white cells instead of red cell casts, and glomeruli are spared until late.
prerequisites: Nephron segments, the renal interstitium, and the urine concentrating mechanism (countercurrent multiplication and the vasa recta)
Renal blood supply, including the low-flow, hypoxic medulla
Hypersensitivity types I to IV and the hapten concept
Urinalysis and urine sediment: pyuria, casts, and their sites of formation
Acute pyelonephritis, urinary obstruction, and kidney stones (UR-12-C)

connections.to: Tubulointerstitial disease and acute kidney injury (UR-12-B)
connections.how: Acute interstitial nephritis is the immune counterpart of acute tubular necrosis, and the urine sediment separates the two.
Obstruction and stones set up chronic pyelonephritis, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, and papillary necrosis.
Drug-induced interstitial nephritis is a hapten-driven, mainly T cell mediated (type IV) reaction with eosinophil recruitment.
Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic medulla explains papillary necrosis and the concentrating defect in sickle cell disease and trait.
Urease-producing Proteus links struvite staghorn stones to chronic destructive infection of the kidney.

terms.def: Inflammation that primarily involves the renal tubules and the interstitium between them, with the glomeruli spared or affected only late.
Acute kidney injury caused by inflammatory cells and edema in the renal interstitium, most often a hypersensitivity reaction to a drug.

Retrograde flow of bladder urine into the ureter and renal pelvis because the ureterovesical valve fails.

Dilated atrophic tubules filled with eosinophilic hyaline casts that resemble thyroid follicles, typical of chronic pyelonephritis.

blocks.text: The renal interstitium is the connective tissue space between tubules and peritubular capillaries. Inflammation there injures tubules and compresses peritubular blood flow, so tubular function and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) fall even though the glomeruli themselves are normal. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) has several causes, including infection and systemic immune diseases, but drugs are the most common cause in adults.
Mechanism: a drug hypersensitivity in the interstitium

The drug or one of its metabolites acts as a hapten. It is secreted or filtered into the tubules, binds proteins of tubular cells or the tubular basement membrane, and makes them immunogenic. Sensitized T cells then drive a delayed, mainly type IV reaction that recruits macrophages and eosinophils. Raised serum IgE and tissue eosinophils in some patients suggest an added type I component. Because the reaction is immune rather than toxic, it is not dose dependent, it begins after a sensitization period of days to weeks (often about 2 weeks), and it recurs quickly on re-exposure to the same or a related drug.

blocks.title: Drugs that commonly cause acute interstitial nephritis
rows: Penicillins (methicillin is the classic example), ampicillin, cephalosporins
blocks.caption: Any new drug started in the preceding weeks is a suspect; these are the classes tested most often.

blocks.title: From new drug to acute kidney injury
steps: New drug started
Drug binds tubular proteins and acts as a hapten
Sensitized T cells recruit macrophages and eosinophils
Interstitial edema and tubulitis
Tubular dysfunction and fall in GFR
Pyuria, WBC casts, rising creatinine
blocks.caption: Removing the drug removes the antigen; persistent inflammation organizes into interstitial fibrosis.

blocks.text: Microscopically the interstitium shows edema and an infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages with prominent eosinophils, and inflammatory cells invade the tubular epithelium (tubulitis). Some drugs, such as methicillin and thiazides, produce small non-necrotizing granulomas. The glomeruli are normal, with one exception: NSAIDs can cause AIN together with a minimal change pattern of podocyte injury and nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Manifestations explained by mechanism

Systemic hypersensitivity produces fever, a maculopapular rash, and blood eosinophilia, but the full triad appears in only a minority of patients, and NSAID-induced AIN often lacks all three. The renal findings follow from where the inflammation sits. Leukocytes cross into the tubule lumen, giving sterile pyuria, and become trapped in Tamm-Horsfall protein to form WBC casts, which place the inflammation inside the kidney. Injured tubules fail to reclaim filtered low molecular weight protein, giving mild proteinuria, and may cause microscopic hematuria, sodium wasting, hyperkalemia, or a normal anion gap acidosis. Edema can enlarge the kidneys. Urine eosinophils are neither sensitive nor specific. Creatinine usually returns toward baseline over weeks once the drug is stopped; prolonged exposure leaves interstitial fibrosis and chronic kidney disease.

blocks.title: Urine sediment in common causes of acute kidney injury
rows: New drug days to weeks earlier; rash, fever, eosinophilia
Fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness
Muddy brown granular and epithelial cell casts
blocks.caption: WBC casts localize inflammation to the kidney; RBC casts localize bleeding to the glomerulus.

blocks.predict: A patient has pyuria and WBC casts, a negative culture, and no rash or eosinophilia, and has taken an NSAID daily for 4 months. Can this be AIN?
blocks.explain: Yes. AIN is defined by interstitial inflammation, not by the systemic triad. NSAID-induced AIN often begins after months and usually lacks fever, rash, and eosinophilia, and it may be accompanied by nephrotic-range proteinuria from a minimal change lesion.

sections.title: Chronic analgesic nephropathy and renal papillary necrosis

blocks.text: The renal papilla is the tip of a medullary pyramid, where collecting ducts empty into a minor calyx. Its only blood supply is the vasa recta, long hairpin capillaries that descend from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary glomeruli. Medullary flow is a small fraction of renal blood flow and moves slowly, which preserves the countercurrent concentration gradient but leaves the papilla hypoxic and hypertonic even in health. Medullary interstitial cells make vasodilating prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGI2) that help sustain this flow, especially when renal perfusion falls.
How combination analgesics destroy the papilla

Analgesic nephropathy follows years of heavy use of combination analgesics, classically phenacetin with aspirin and caffeine. Phenacetin is metabolized to acetaminophen, which the countercurrent system concentrates in the papilla. There its oxidative metabolites injure cells. Aspirin adds two insults: it depletes glutathione, the main defense against those metabolites, and it inhibits cyclooxygenase, removing prostaglandin vasodilation from an already marginal circulation. The combination is therefore more damaging than either drug alone. The papillae die first; the cortex that drains through each necrotic papilla then undergoes tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, giving chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis.

blocks.title: Analgesic nephropathy
steps: Years of combination analgesic use
Acetaminophen concentrated in the papilla by countercurrent
Aspirin depletes glutathione; oxidative injury proceeds
Aspirin blocks prostaglandin vasodilation; papillary ischemia
Papillary necrosis
Overlying cortex atrophies and scars
blocks.caption: Toxic injury and ischemia converge on the most poorly perfused tissue in the kidney.

blocks.text: Grossly, the necrotic papillae are shrunken and yellow-brown and may calcify or slough, and the cortex above them forms depressed scars. Microscopy shows coagulative necrosis of the papillae with ghost outlines of tubules, and tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and chronic inflammation in the overlying cortex.

The clinical picture follows the anatomy. Loss of the inner medulla destroys the concentration gradient early, causing polyuria and nocturia. Inflamed tissue sheds white cells, giving sterile pyuria, and hematuria is common. A sloughed papilla can enter the ureter and cause colic, gross hematuria, or obstruction, and superimposed infection is frequent. Creatinine rises slowly, and hypertension may develop. Long-term phenacetin use also increases the risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.

blocks.title: Causes of renal papillary necrosis
rows: Concentrated toxic metabolites plus loss of prostaglandin vasodilation
Small vessel disease of the medulla, often combined with acute pyelonephritis
Red cells sickle in the hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic medulla and occlude the vasa recta
Intense inflammation and edema compress papillary blood flow
Raised pelvic pressure lowers medullary blood flow, often with infection
blocks.caption: Every cause attacks the same weak point: the slow, low-oxygen blood supply of the papillary tip.

blocks.title: Hematuria in sickle cell trait
blocks.text: A 22-year-old man with sickle cell trait has painless gross hematuria and passes a small piece of tissue. His first morning urine is dilute. Step 1: in sickle cell trait less than half of each red cell's hemoglobin is hemoglobin S, so sickling elsewhere needs extreme conditions. Step 2: the papilla is the exception; low oxygen tension, high osmolality, and low pH there promote polymerization of hemoglobin S. Step 3: sickled cells occlude the slow vasa recta, so the papillary tip infarcts and can slough, causing bleeding. Step 4: vasa recta loss also dissipates the medullary gradient, so the urine cannot be concentrated even before papillae slough. The same medullary conditions explain papillary necrosis from analgesics and diabetes.

sections.title: Chronic pyelonephritis: reflux nephropathy and chronic obstruction

blocks.text: Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring that involves the calyces and pelvis as well as the parenchyma. Calyceal involvement is what separates it from other chronic tubulointerstitial diseases. It develops by two main routes: reflux nephropathy, which begins in childhood, and chronic obstruction with recurrent infection.
Reflux nephropathy

Normally the ureter crosses the bladder wall obliquely, and this intravesical segment is compressed when the bladder contracts, acting as a one-way flap valve. A congenitally short intravesical segment, or bladder outlet obstruction and neurogenic bladder that raise voiding pressure, lets urine reflux up the ureter. Sterile reflux at normal bladder pressures causes little injury; most damage comes when infected bladder urine reaches the pelvis and then enters the parenchyma. That entry depends on papillary shape. Simple papillae are convex with slit-like duct openings that close under pressure, whereas compound papillae, concentrated at the upper and lower poles, are flat or concave with wide openings that stay open, so intrarenal reflux and the worst scars occur at the poles.

blocks.title: Reflux nephropathy
steps: Incompetent ureterovesical valve
Infected bladder urine refluxes into the renal pelvis
Intrarenal reflux through polar compound papillae
Acute pyelonephritis destroys papillae and tubules
Cortex contracts into a scar over a blunted calyx
Hypertension, polyuria, and progressive chronic kidney disease
blocks.caption: Repeated episodes, often beginning in early childhood, add scar to scar.

blocks.text: In chronic obstructive pyelonephritis, stones, prostatic enlargement, strictures, or congenital anomalies cause stasis, and stagnant urine permits recurrent infection above the obstruction. Back pressure also injures the medulla directly. The process is unilateral or bilateral depending on the level of the obstruction.
Morphology

The kidneys are irregularly and often asymmetrically scarred. Each scar is a coarse, discrete corticomedullary depression lying directly over a dilated, blunted, deformed calyx, because the infection destroyed the papilla and the cortex that drains into it. Microscopically there is uneven interstitial fibrosis with lymphocytes and plasma cells, and neutrophils during flares. Tubules are atrophic or dilated, and the dilated ones fill with eosinophilic hyaline casts that resemble thyroid colloid (thyroidization). The calyceal wall is chronically inflamed and fibrotic, and glomeruli show periglomerular fibrosis. Thyroidization occurs in other chronic tubular diseases, so it supports the diagnosis only alongside the gross pattern.

blocks.title: Patterns of renal scarring
rows: Scars over necrotic papillae, usually bilateral
blocks.caption: Calyceal deformity under a coarse scar points to pyelonephritis; uniform fine granularity points to vascular disease.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow from tubulointerstitial loss. Destruction of the medulla causes polyuria and nocturia, scarring and ischemia stimulate renin release and hypertension, and nephron loss slowly reduces GFR. Proteinuria is mild at first, but surviving nephrons hyperfilter and develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which brings heavier proteinuria and faster progression. Bacteriuria and WBC casts appear during flares. Reflux nephropathy is an important cause of hypertension and chronic kidney disease in children and young adults, and it can be clinically silent until those complications appear.

blocks.predict: Two kidneys are equally small. One has a coarse polar scar over a blunted calyx; the other has a finely granular surface and normal calyces. Which disease made each?
blocks.explain: Infection that destroys a papilla shrinks the cortex draining through it and deforms the calyx, giving coarse focal scars over abnormal calyces (chronic pyelonephritis). Hyaline arteriolosclerosis narrows small vessels throughout the cortex, giving uniform fine scarring with intact calyces (benign nephrosclerosis).

blocks.text: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is an uncommon, chronic, destructive form of pyelonephritis that is almost always unilateral. Its usual setting is long-standing obstruction by a stone, often a staghorn calculus, with infection by Proteus or Escherichia coli. Proteus links the two: its urease splits urea into ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and precipitating struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), which grows into a branching stone that fills the pelvis and calyces and harbors bacteria within it.

blocks.title: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
steps: Urease-producing Proteus infects the urine
Ammonia alkalinizes urine; struvite staghorn stone forms
Obstruction prevents drainage; infection persists
Parenchyma is destroyed; macrophages ingest lipid debris
Foamy macrophage nodules replace the kidney
Enlarged, nonfunctioning kidney with a mass
blocks.caption: Obstruction converts a treatable infection into chronic, nonresolving inflammation.

blocks.text: Because the obstructed kidney cannot drain, suppurative inflammation never resolves and steadily destroys the parenchyma. Macrophages engulf lipid released from necrotic cell membranes and fill with it, becoming foamy xanthoma cells. Grossly the kidney is enlarged and its parenchyma is replaced by yellow-orange nodules and abscess cavities arranged around dilated calyces containing the stone. Microscopically sheets of foamy macrophages mix with plasma cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and multinucleated giant cells. The process can extend into the perinephric fat and occasionally forms fistulas.

Patients present with flank pain, fever, malaise, weight loss, a palpable mass, and a history of recurrent urinary infection, often with anemia and leukocytosis. Imaging shows an enlarged kidney that does not function, with a stone and a mass. Each of these features can also be explained by renal cell carcinoma, which is why the lesion is a classic mimic. The resemblance extends to the microscope, where pale foamy macrophages can look like the clear cells of clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry separates them: macrophages express the histiocyte marker CD68, whereas carcinoma cells express epithelial markers such as cytokeratin and PAX8. Malakoplakia, another macrophage disorder of the urinary tract linked to defective bacterial killing, is distinguished by Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, which xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis lacks.

blocks.title: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis versus clear cell renal cell carcinoma
rows: Neoplasm, often with VHL gene loss
Usually absent; fever can occur as a paraneoplastic sign
Tumor cells with lipid and glycogen (cytokeratin and PAX8 positive)
blocks.caption: Both present as a renal mass with pale cells; the stone, the infection, and the inflammatory mixture favor xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

blocks.text: The bladder is lined by urothelium whose superficial umbrella cells are joined by tight junctions and covered by uroplakin plaques and a glycosaminoglycan layer. Together these form one of the tightest barriers in the body, keeping urea, potassium, and acid out of the bladder wall. Afferent nerves in the wall signal fullness, mainly through the pelvic nerves to sacral segments S2 to S4, and the same fibers can signal pain when they are sensitized.

Interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome, is chronic pain, pressure, or discomfort perceived as coming from the bladder, accompanied by urgency and frequency, in the absence of infection or another identifiable cause. It is much more common in women and often coexists with other chronic pain disorders, such as irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia. Its cause is not established, but the leading explanations interact in a self-sustaining loop.

blocks.title: Proposed self-sustaining loop in interstitial cystitis
steps: Defective glycosaminoglycan layer; leaky urothelium
Urine potassium enters the bladder wall
Sensory nerves depolarize; mast cells release mediators
Neurogenic inflammation and nerve sensitization
Further urothelial injury; barrier stays leaky
blocks.caption: Barrier failure, mast cell activation, and neural sensitization are linked hypotheses, not a proven sequence.

blocks.text: Patients fall into two broad groups at cystoscopy. A minority have Hunner lesions, reddened mucosal areas with small vessels radiating toward a central scar, which may crack and bleed when the bladder is distended. Biopsies from this group show chronic inflammation with lymphocytes and plasma cells, granulation tissue, and increased mast cells in the detrusor, and advanced cases develop transmural fibrosis and a small, contracted bladder. The larger group has a normal-looking bladder or only petechial hemorrhages after distention, a nonspecific finding.

The symptoms follow from a sensitized bladder. Pain rises as the bladder fills and eases after voiding, so patients void often and in small volumes, day and night, to keep pain down. Urgency here is a pressure to relieve pain rather than fear of leakage, which helps separate it from overactive bladder. Dyspareunia and pelvic floor pain are common. Urinalysis and culture are repeatedly negative, so the diagnosis is made by excluding conditions that cause the same symptoms.

blocks.title: Conditions that resemble interstitial cystitis
rows: Positive culture, pyuria, and nitrite; symptoms resolve when infection clears
Frequency and urgency with hematuria; malignant cells on urine cytology or biopsy
Hematuria and a stone on imaging
Urgency driven by fear of leakage, often with incontinence, without pain
History of pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide, or ketamine use
blocks.caption: Interstitial cystitis is a diagnosis of exclusion; carcinoma in situ is the most dangerous condition to miss.

blocks.title: Why a sterile urine does not rule out disease
blocks.text: A 45-year-old woman has 2 years of suprapubic pain that worsens as her bladder fills and eases after voiding, with frequency and nocturia. Five cultures are negative. Step 1: negative cultures exclude bacterial cystitis, but not every inflammatory or neoplastic cause. Step 2: carcinoma in situ also causes frequency and urgency with sterile urine, so urine cytology and cystoscopy are needed. Step 3: if cytology is negative and cystoscopy shows a red patch with radiating vessels, a Hunner lesion is likely; biopsy showing chronic inflammation and mast cells, without malignant cells, completes the exclusion. Step 4: the pattern of pain with filling and relief after emptying points to bladder sensory sensitization rather than detrusor overactivity.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain where these diseases strike. The papilla depends on slow vasa recta flow and prostaglandin vasodilation, so analgesics, sickling, diabetes, and inflammation kill it first and concentrating ability fails early. Papillary shape decides where reflux enters the kidney, and the oblique ureterovesical course decides whether reflux happens at all. Immunology explains drug-induced AIN as hapten-driven T cell hypersensitivity, and microbiology explains why Proteus urease builds the staghorn stones behind xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

Pathology ties them together as tubulointerstitial disease: inflammation between tubules produces pyuria, WBC casts, tubular proteinuria, and polyuria rather than the RBC casts and heavy proteinuria of glomerular disease, until secondary glomerulosclerosis develops late. The limits matter. The hypersensitivity triad is often absent, thyroidization is not specific, foamy cells can mimic carcinoma, and interstitial cystitis has no confirmatory test, so each diagnosis rests on the full pattern rather than a single finding.

summary: Drug-induced AIN is a hapten-driven, mainly T cell mediated reaction days to weeks after a drug, with interstitial edema, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and spared glomeruli.
AIN gives sterile pyuria, WBC casts, and rising creatinine; fever, rash, and eosinophilia occur together in only a minority, and NSAID cases may add minimal change proteinuria.
WBC casts localize inflammation to the kidney (AIN or pyelonephritis); RBC casts localize disease to the glomerulus.
The papilla is the most poorly perfused part of the kidney, which is why it dies first from analgesics, diabetes, sickle cell disease or trait, severe pyelonephritis, and obstruction.

Analgesic nephropathy combines concentrated acetaminophen metabolites, glutathione depletion, and loss of prostaglandin vasodilation, and it raises the risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
Chronic pyelonephritis arises from reflux or obstruction with recurrent infection and produces coarse, asymmetric scars over blunted calyces, worst at the poles in reflux.
Thyroidization (dilated tubules filled with eosinophilic casts) with calyceal deformity is the classic histology; hypertension, polyuria, and secondary FSGS follow.
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is unilateral destruction by foamy macrophages behind an obstructing stone, usually with Proteus, and mimics clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

Interstitial cystitis is chronic bladder pain that rises with filling, with urgency, frequency, and negative cultures, mostly in women; a minority have Hunner lesions, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

verify: Onset of drug-induced AIN is given as about 2 weeks (Robbins gives an average near 15 days with a wide range); NSAID cases can begin after months. Confirm the timing NABNE expects.

The proportion of AIN patients with the full triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia is quoted from about 5% to 10% in some sources and higher in older series; this chapter states only that it is a minority.

Phenacetin has been withdrawn in many countries; confirm whether NABNE expects phenacetin by name and whether it tests analgesic nephropathy from single-agent NSAIDs or acetaminophen, where the evidence is less consistent.
The proportion of interstitial cystitis patients with Hunner lesions varies widely among series (roughly 5% to 50% depending on population and definition); confirm the figure NABNE uses, if any.
Symptom-duration criteria for interstitial cystitis (for example more than 6 weeks in some guidelines and 6 months in others) differ between organizations.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Hunner lesion, Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, or only the descriptive terms.
The interstitial cystitis loop (glycosaminoglycan defect, potassium leak, mast cell activation, neural sensitization) presents leading hypotheses, not an established pathogenesis.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: papillae-reflux (simple versus compound papilla with duct orifices and polar scars) and renal-scar-patterns (chronic pyelonephritis versus nephrosclerosis versus papillary necrosis on a bisected kidney).
